attribution: Marcel Breuer, Club chair (model B3 / Wassily), 1927–1928, chrome-plated tubular steel and canvas. The Museum of Modern Art, Gift of Herbert Bayer, 229.1934. Public object-page image; no general reuse license granted by this package.
rights_evidence: The exact MoMA object page publishes this image and directs reproduction requests to Art Resource/Scala. No CC or unrestricted reuse license is stated. It must not inherit the replaced Lorkan photograph’s CC BY 2.0 license.
claim_scope: Historical Bauhaus tubular-furniture branch: a single documented museum object exposes frame, flexible contact bands and voids clearly. Not a universal Bauhaus color/material recipe or authentication of another chair.
limits: This is the single MoMA accession 229.1934, catalogued 1927–1928, not the three later display chairs in the replaced photo. MoMA attributes the manufacturer to Standard Möbel rather than establishing it unconditionally. The image clearly shows exposed steel members and black bands, while canvas composition and date are documented facts. It cannot establish hidden connectors, load performance or the age/manufacturer/authorization of a newly supplied chair. A white background, black sling or steel tube alone is not a Bauhaus membership test.
observable_features: A single complete chair is isolated against a pale neutral background, without other chairs, windows, display labels or strong projected shadows.
Bent reflective tubular members trace the open perimeter and continuous floor-level support relationships.
Separate dark seat, back and arm bands bridge the metal members instead of enclosing the frame in a padded solid mass.
Thin contact bands, repeating rails and large intervening gaps separate the sitter’s surfaces from the support outline.

association_evidence.supports: MoMA identifies this exact B3/Wassily accession 229.1934 as 1927–1928, chrome-plated tubular steel and canvas, Gift of Herbert Bayer, with manufacture attributed to Standard Möbel. Its discussion separately locates the earlier 1925 version in Breuer’s Bauhaus teaching period. Its licensing section establishes that the public preview is not a stated open image license.
